name: Futurism
scope: The Futurist movement founded by Filippo Tommaso Marinetti in Italy with the 1909 Manifesto of Futurism: the doctrine its manifestos set out (rejection of the past and of cultural institutions, glorification of technology, speed, youth, violence and war, ardent Italian nationalism) and the political agenda the defining sources describe as part of it from the start (1913 political programme, the 1918 Futurist Political Party, interventionism, the alliance with the early Fasci di Combattimento). Its defining sources are encyclopedias and scholarship on the movement (Britannica, the Routledge Encyclopedia of Modernism, Berghaus's account in a Gale encyclopedia, Tate) and the movement's own manifestos. Excludes Russian Futurism and Cubo-Futurism (the Routledge entry and Wikipedia describe it as ideologically opposed or a separate movement, tied to the Bolshevik cause), futurology and Futures studies, and the narrower Italian Fascism, whose own sources do not answer for Futurism.

summary: Futurism, as Marinetti launched it in 1909, rejects the past and the institutions that preserve it (museums, libraries, academies) and glorifies technology, speed, youth, violence and war. Its sources tie it to an intense Italian nationalism, support for entering the First World War, and a political programme of national regeneration through revolution; they record no settled positions on most economic, social or constitutional questions.

war-builds-character.rationale: The founding manifesto glorifies war as 'the world's only hygiene'; the Encyclopedia.com entry says Marinetti saw war as a purifying and revitalizing force that restores health to the body politic.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: The manifesto glorifies 'the destructive gesture of freedom-bringers' and holds art to be violence; Marinetti's political ideology treats regenerative violence as the cure for decay.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Marinetti equated 'futurism = revolution = war' and the manifesto sings of 'the tides of revolution in the modern capitals'.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: The manifesto says 'We will destroy the museums, libraries, academies of every kind' and urges setting fire to library shelves; the painters call to 'destroy the cult of the past'.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The movement set out to free Italy from its museums and from 'the cult of the past'; the painters condemn 'hired restorers' and the architecture manifesto despises the reconstruction of ancient monuments.

accelerate-technology.rationale: The manifesto and painters' manifesto exalt speed, machines and science, and the architecture manifesto says architecture 'now makes a break with tradition'; Routledge describes values 'derived from the innovations of technology' set against traditional institutions.

restore-past-order.rationale: The manifesto asks 'Why should we look back?' and the painters want the threshold of the future 'swept free of mummies'.

gradual-change.rationale: The manifesto is called 'violently upsetting' and 'incendiary', and condemns compromise; the architecture manifesto says 'Everything must be revolutionized'.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Futurism rejects respect for established institutions: it would destroy museums and academies, and the architecture manifesto declares every generation must build its own city.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The manifesto sings of factories, railway stations, shipyards and locomotives, and the painters hail the 'millions of machines' roaring in Italy.

national-rebirth.rationale: The painters' manifesto says 'Italy is being reborn' after being 'a land of the dead'; Encyclopedia.com describes a programme of political, intellectual and moral regeneration.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Encyclopedia.com says Marinetti held the unification of Italy would be complete only when the 'terra irredenta' were liberated from Austrian domination.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: The manifesto glorifies war and militarism, and the movement staged demonstrations for Italy's entry into the First World War, a war to take the unredeemed territories.

initiating-nondefensive-force-unjustifie.rationale: The manifesto glorifies war and militarism as ends, and the movement campaigned for Italy to join a war it could have stayed out of.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The manifesto glorifies militarism and patriotism.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: The manifesto glorifies war and 'beautiful ideas worth dying for'; Futurists urged intervention and many enlisted.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: The movement was patriotic and campaigned for its own country's entry into the war, so it rejects working for one's own government's defeat.

parliament-supreme.rationale: TheArtStory says the Futurists, like the Fascists, were opposed to parliamentary democracy; the other sources are silent, so the position is weakly stated.

notes: Most statements are null: the sources describe the movement's art, its glorification of war and its nationalism, but give no position on economic or constitutional questions. De-Vaticanisation (1931) is by Florentine Futurists writing as Fascists and is not used for answers.
